parsedSyllabus.subject: Art & Design
assessmentObjectives: Understanding art: recognise and respond to the work of artists and their own/others' art
Making art: use materials, tools and techniques to create art
Reflecting and evaluating: talk about art using simple describing words
Thinking and working artistically: explore, experiment and make choices as an artist

unit-1.title: Marks, Lines and Shapes
unit-1.description: Exploring what different tools and materials can do, and looking closely at the world around us.

lessons.title: Lesson 1 -- Exploring Marks and Lines
lessons.objectives: Explore different mark-making tools and describe the lines and marks they make (thick/thin, straight/wavy/zigzag/dotted); begin to talk about what we see and make.

steps.title: What is a mark?
steps.definition: A mark is anything we make on paper -- a dot, a line, a scribble, a splodge. Different tools make different marks.
steps.example: A pencil makes a thin, scratchy line. A thick paintbrush makes a wide, soft line. A cotton bud dipped in paint makes small round dots.

cards.label: Straight line
cards.content: A line that goes directly from one point to another, with no bends.

cards.label: Wavy line
cards.content: A line that curves up and down, like the sea.

cards.label: Zigzag line
cards.content: A line that goes sharply up and down, like a lightning bolt.

cards.label: Dotted line
cards.content: A line made of lots of small dots close together.

cards.question: This mark is thick and soft, with rounded edges.
cards.answer: A big paintbrush! Big brushes make thick, soft marks.

cards.question: This mark is a row of small round dots.
cards.answer: A cotton bud, or the tip of a pencil, dipped in paint!

summaryPoints: A mark is anything we make on paper.
Different tools make different kinds of marks: thick, thin, straight, wavy, zigzag, dotted.
homeworkItems: Look for lines around your house or garden -- on tiles, on leaves, on the road -- and remember one to tell the class.

teachingScript.overview: Let children experiment with real tools first, then give them words for what they discover -- naming follows exploring, not the other way round.

talkingPoints: Have a pencil, a thick brush and a cotton bud out and let children guess what mark each will make before you demonstrate.
Trace each line type in the air with your whole arm before naming it -- straight arm, wavy wiggle, sharp zigzag.
Hold up real marked paper samples if you have them; let children guess the tool before revealing.
misconceptions: Children may think only pencils make "real" drawing marks -- emphasise that paint, chalk and even fingers are valid mark-making tools.

talkingPoints: Have children draw one line type each in the air as a quick recap before moving to the worksheet.

quizQuestions.question: Which word describes a line that curves up and down like the sea?
A cotton bud dipped in paint makes marks that are...

flashcards.definition: Anything we make on paper -- a dot, a line, a scribble.
A line with no bends, going directly from one point to another.
A line that curves up and down.
A line that goes sharply up and down.

worksheetContent.title: Worksheet -- Exploring Marks and Lines
worksheetContent.instructions: Draw with a grown-up or teacher's help. There is no wrong answer -- just have fun making marks!

questions.prompt: Draw one straight line, one wavy line, and one zigzag line.
Use a cotton bud (or your fingertip) to make five dotty marks.
Tell a grown-up: which mark was your favourite to make, and why?

lessons.title: Lesson 2 -- Looking Closely and Drawing What We See
lessons.objectives: Look closely at a natural object and notice its shape, edge and small details; make an observational drawing; begin to use simple art words to describe what we see.

steps.title: Looking closely
steps.definition: Looking closely means noticing small details -- the edges, the shape, the little lines and bumps -- before we draw.
steps.example: A leaf might look green and simple from far away, but up close it has a pointed tip, a bumpy edge, and thin lines running through it.

cards.definition: The outside line of a shape.
The thin lines inside a leaf that carry water, like tiny rivers.
The pointed end of a leaf.

items.label: A coin
items.reason: A coin has a smooth, curved edge all the way round -- no corners.

items.label: A mango leaf
items.reason: A mango leaf has a sharp, pointed tip at one end.

items.label: A spiral shell
items.reason: A spiral shell curls round and round with no sharp corners.

items.label: A starfruit slice
items.reason: A starfruit slice has several sharp points around its edge.

summaryPoints: Looking closely means noticing edges, shapes and small details before we draw.
We can describe what we see using words like edge, vein and tip.
homeworkItems: Find one leaf or shell at home and look closely at its edge -- is it round, pointed, or bumpy?

teachingScript.overview: Bring in real leaves (or shells/pebbles) for children to hold and examine before drawing -- touch and looking together builds richer observational drawings than looking alone.

talkingPoints: Pass round a real leaf and ask children what they notice before you name any parts.
Point to the edge, vein and tip on the real leaf as each word is revealed.
Use real local objects where possible -- a shell from the beach, a coin, a starfruit slice -- rather than only pictures.
misconceptions: Children may sort by size rather than by round/pointed edges -- redirect attention to the outline shape specifically.

talkingPoints: Ask two or three children to describe their own leaf's edge in one word.

quizQuestions.question: What do we call the outside line of a shape?
A spiral shell has an edge that is...

flashcards.definition: Looking closely and noticing small details.
The outside line of a shape.
The thin lines inside a leaf.
The pointed end of a leaf.

worksheetContent.title: Worksheet -- Looking Closely and Drawing What We See
worksheetContent.instructions: Look at your real leaf or shell very closely before you start drawing.

questions.prompt: Draw your leaf or shell as carefully as you can. Try to copy its real edge.
Is your object's edge round or pointed? Circle the word: ROUND / POINTED.
Tell a grown-up one small detail you noticed that you almost missed.

unit-2.title: Colour and Painting
unit-2.description: Primary colours, colour mixing, and painting techniques.

lessons.title: Lesson 3 -- Primary Colours
lessons.objectives: Name the three primary colours (red, yellow, blue); understand that primary colours cannot be made by mixing; predict what happens when two primary colours are mixed.

steps.title: Primary colours
steps.definition: Primary colours are red, yellow and blue. They are special because we can't make them by mixing any other colours together.
steps.example: Every other colour -- orange, green, purple, brown -- is made by mixing primary colours together in different amounts.

cards.label: Red
cards.content: Like a hibiscus flower, or a stop sign.

cards.label: Yellow
cards.content: Like the sun, or a ripe mango.

cards.label: Blue
cards.content: Like the sea, or a clear sky.

cards.question: If we mix red and yellow paint together, what colour do we get?
If we mix blue and yellow paint together, what colour do we get?

summaryPoints: Red, yellow and blue are the three primary colours.
Mixing two primary colours makes a new colour: red+yellow=orange, blue+yellow=green.
homeworkItems: Look for something red, something yellow and something blue on your way home.

teachingScript.overview: Let children mix real paint with their fingers or a brush before confirming the rule -- discovery first, naming second, just like the marks lesson.

talkingPoints: Show three pots of paint: red, yellow, blue. Ask if anyone can guess why these three are special.
Ask children for their own local examples of each colour before revealing the given ones.
Actually mix the paints in front of the class after each guess, so the reveal is a real demonstration, not just words.
misconceptions: Children sometimes think mixing any two colours always makes brown or black -- show a clean red+yellow mix to counter this early.

talkingPoints: Ask the class to chant the three primary colours together.

quizQuestions.question: Which three colours are the primary colours?
Mixing blue and yellow paint makes...

flashcards.definition: A colour that cannot be made by mixing other colours -- red, yellow, and blue.
Combining two colours together to make a new colour.
Made by mixing red and yellow.
Made by mixing blue and yellow.

worksheetContent.title: Worksheet -- Primary Colours
worksheetContent.instructions: Use red, yellow and blue paint or crayons for this worksheet.

questions.prompt: Colour the three circles: one red, one yellow, one blue.
Mix red and yellow in the box. What colour did you make?
Draw one thing from home that is a primary colour.

lessons.title: Lesson 4 -- Painting Techniques
lessons.objectives: Explore and name different ways of using a paintbrush (dabbing, sweeping, dry-brush); choose a technique on purpose to create an effect.

steps.title: A painting technique is a way of using the brush
steps.definition: A technique is a special way of using a tool. With a paintbrush, we can dab, sweep, or use a nearly-dry brush -- each way makes a different effect.
steps.example: Dabbing the brush up and down makes little spots, like leaves on a tree. Sweeping it sideways makes long, smooth strokes, like the sky.

cards.label: Dabbing
cards.content: Touching the brush up and down without dragging it -- good for leaves, dots, and texture.

cards.label: Sweeping
cards.content: Dragging the brush smoothly across the paper -- good for sky, water, and big open spaces.

cards.label: Dry-brush
cards.content: Using a brush with very little paint on it -- makes a rough, scratchy texture, good for grass or fur.

questions.question: You want to paint a fluffy cat's fur. Which technique is best?
questions.feedback: ✓ Dry-brush makes a rough, scratchy texture that looks like fur.

questions.question: You want to paint a smooth blue sky. Which technique is best?
questions.feedback: ✓ Sweeping the brush makes long, smooth strokes, perfect for open sky.

summaryPoints: A technique is a special way of using a tool.
Dabbing, sweeping and dry-brush each make a different effect.
homeworkItems: Practise dabbing and sweeping with a dry paintbrush (no paint) on paper at home.

teachingScript.overview: Demonstrate all three techniques live on a shared sheet before children try them on their own paper, so they see the physical brush movement, not just hear it described.

talkingPoints: Do a real dab and a real sweep on the board/shared paper before naming either.
Physically demonstrate dry-brush too -- wipe most of the paint off the brush first so the difference is obvious.
Let children mime the brush movement with an empty hand before answering each question.
Ask three children to each demonstrate one technique in the air.

quizQuestions.question: Touching the brush up and down without dragging it is called...
Which technique is best for painting a smooth, open sky?

flashcards.definition: A special way of using a tool to make a certain effect.
Touching the brush up and down without dragging it.
Dragging the brush smoothly across the paper.
Using a brush with very little paint for a rough, scratchy texture.

worksheetContent.title: Worksheet -- Painting Techniques
worksheetContent.instructions: Try each technique in its own box before starting your picture.

questions.prompt: Practise dabbing in the first box, sweeping in the second box, and dry-brush in the third box.
Paint a small picture using at least two different techniques.
Tell a grown-up which technique you used for which part of your picture.

unit-3.title: Pattern and Print
unit-3.description: Printmaking with everyday objects and repeating patterns.

lessons.title: Lesson 5 -- Printing with Everyday Objects
lessons.objectives: Understand that printing means pressing a shape onto paper to leave a repeated mark; explore printing with everyday and natural objects.

steps.title: What is printing?
steps.definition: Printing means covering an object with paint and pressing it onto paper. It leaves a copy of the object's shape -- and we can print the same shape again and again.
steps.example: If you dip a bottle cap in paint and press it on paper, you get a neat circle. Press it again next to the first one, and you get two matching circles.

cards.label: Sponge piece
cards.content: Makes a soft, textured square or blob shape.

cards.label: Leaf
cards.content: Makes a shape with veins showing through, just like the real leaf.

cards.label: Fingertip
cards.content: Makes a small round print with your own fingerprint pattern inside it.

cards.question: If I press a leaf covered in paint onto paper, what will the print show?
cards.answer: The leaf's shape, edge and veins -- a real copy of the leaf!

cards.question: If I press my fingertip covered in paint onto paper, what will the print show?
cards.answer: A small circle with your own special fingerprint pattern inside it.

summaryPoints: Printing means pressing a paint-covered object onto paper.
The same object makes the same shape every time we print it.
homeworkItems: Find one safe object at home that you think would make an interesting print shape.

teachingScript.overview: Set up 3-4 printing stations (sponge, leaf, bottle cap, fingertip) so children rotate and compare prints directly, rather than only imagining the difference.

talkingPoints: Demonstrate one print live before explaining, so the idea is anchored to something they just watched.
Have real examples of each object at the front so children can predict the print shape by looking at the object first.
Compare a leaf print to the real leaf side by side -- the vein pattern transferring is a lovely moment to pause on.
Ask two children to name a printing object they'd like to try next.

quizQuestions.question: Printing means...
options: Drawing a picture with a pencil
Pressing a paint-covered object onto paper

quizQuestions.question: A leaf print will show the leaf's...

flashcards.definition: Pressing a paint-covered object onto paper to leave a copy of its shape.
The mark left behind after pressing an object onto paper.

worksheetContent.title: Worksheet -- Printing with Everyday Objects
worksheetContent.instructions: Use safe household or natural objects and paint (with adult help) to make your prints.

questions.prompt: Make three different prints using three different objects.
Which print shape surprised you the most?
Draw a circle around the print you like best.

lessons.title: Lesson 6 -- Repeating Patterns
lessons.objectives: Understand that a pattern repeats a shape, colour or object in the same order again and again; predict what comes next in a simple pattern; create a printed repeating pattern.

steps.title: What is a pattern?
steps.definition: A pattern repeats a shape, colour or object in the same order, again and again.
steps.example: Red circle, blue circle, red circle, blue circle -- that's a pattern because red and blue keep repeating in the same order.

cards.definition: To happen again in the same way.

questions.question: Red, blue, red, blue, red, ___?
questions.feedback: ✓ The pattern repeats red-blue-red-blue, so blue comes next.

questions.question: Circle, square, circle, square, circle, ___?
questions.feedback: ✓ The pattern repeats circle-square, so square comes next.

summaryPoints: A pattern repeats a shape, colour or object in the same order.
We can predict what comes next once we spot the repeating order.
homeworkItems: Find a pattern at home -- on clothing, tiles, or a woven mat -- and describe its repeating order to a grown-up.

teachingScript.overview: Build a physical repeating pattern with the class (children standing in a red-blue-red-blue line) before moving to printed patterns on paper.

talkingPoints: Line up a few children alternating two colours of card/clothing to make a human pattern before explaining.
Connect 'sequence' back to the human pattern line -- ask what order the colours went in.
Cover the answer with your hand and let children call out their guess before revealing.
Have children clap a repeating rhythm pattern (clap-clap-stamp, clap-clap-stamp) as a fun physical recap.

quizQuestions.question: A pattern is when something...
options: Repeats in the same order again and again
Is a random mix of anything

quizQuestions.question: Star, star, moon, star, star, moon, star, star, ___?

flashcards.definition: A shape, colour or object that repeats in the same order again and again.
To happen again in the same way.
The order things happen in.

worksheetContent.title: Worksheet -- Repeating Patterns
worksheetContent.instructions: Use your printing objects from Lesson 5, or crayons, to make patterns.

questions.prompt: Print or draw a repeating pattern using two shapes or colours (at least 6 in the row).
Circle the part of your pattern that repeats.
Draw what would come next if your pattern continued.

unit-4.title: Sculpture and Sharing Our Art
unit-4.description: Making 3D art from natural materials, and talking about our own and others' art.

lessons.title: Lesson 7 -- Sculpture with Natural Materials
lessons.objectives: Understand that a sculpture is 3D art that can be seen from every side; explore joining and arranging natural materials to make a sculpture.

steps.title: What is a sculpture?
steps.definition: A sculpture is art you can walk around and see from every side -- not flat like a drawing or painting, but standing up in real space.
steps.example: A sandcastle is a sculpture. A tower built from shells and twigs is a sculpture. You can walk all the way around either one and see something different each time.

cards.label: Shells
cards.content: Hard and curved -- good for a smooth, shiny surface.

cards.label: Twigs
cards.content: Straight and stiff -- good for legs, frames, or spikes.

cards.label: Leaves
cards.content: Flat and bendy -- good for roofs, wings, or covering.

cards.label: Sand
cards.content: Soft and shapeable when wet -- good for a solid base.

cards.question: You want to build a strong, straight tower. Which material is best for the frame?
cards.answer: Twigs! They are straight and stiff, so they hold their shape.

cards.question: You want a smooth, shiny roof for your sculpture. Which material is best?
cards.answer: Shells! Their curved, hard surface catches the light nicely.

summaryPoints: A sculpture is 3D art we can walk around and see from every side.
Different natural materials are good for different parts of a sculpture.
homeworkItems: Collect a few small natural materials (shells, twigs, leaves) for our sculpture-making lesson, if you can find any safely.

teachingScript.overview: Bring in a finished example sculpture (even a simple one) and have children physically walk around it before starting the definition, so '3D' is felt, not just explained.

talkingPoints: Walk the class around a real 3D object (a bag, a plant pot) and ask what looks different from each side.
Let children handle each material and describe it in their own words before revealing the given description.
Encourage children to justify their material choice out loud, not just guess silently.
misconceptions: Children may want to use only one material for everything -- gently prompt them to notice each material's different strengths.

talkingPoints: Ask children to name the material they're most excited to build with.

quizQuestions.question: A sculpture is different from a drawing because...
options: It is 3D and can be seen from every side

quizQuestions.question: Which material is best for a strong, straight tower frame?

flashcards.definition: 3D art that can be seen from every side, not flat like a drawing.
What something is made from, e.g. shells, twigs, leaves, sand.

worksheetContent.title: Worksheet -- Sculpture with Natural Materials
worksheetContent.instructions: Use collected natural materials, or draw them if none are available.

questions.prompt: List (or draw) three natural materials you would like to build a sculpture with.
Build or draw a small sculpture using at least two materials.
Walk around your sculpture (or turn your drawing). Does it look different from the other side?

lessons.title: Lesson 8 -- Sharing and Talking About Our Art
lessons.objectives: Use simple describing words to talk about our own and others' art; practise sharing what we notice, like, and would try differently next time.

steps.title: Talking about art
steps.definition: Reflecting means looking at art -- our own or someone else's -- and using words to say what we notice, what we like, and what we might try differently next time.
steps.example: Instead of just saying "I like it," an artist might say "I notice you used lots of dabbing to make the leaves look fluffy -- I like how bumpy the texture feels."

steps.title: Sentence starters for talking about art

cards.definition: Used to point out something specific you see in the artwork.
Used to say what you enjoy about the artwork and why.
Used to say one thing you might try differently.

questions.question: "I notice you used red and yellow together to make orange." -- is this a good describing sentence?
questions.feedback: ✓ It points out something specific the artist actually did.

questions.question: "It's nice." -- is this a good describing sentence?
options: No -- it could be said about anything, so it's not specific
questions.feedback: ✓ "Nice" could describe anything -- a good describing sentence names something specific you noticed.

summaryPoints: Reflecting means using words to say what we notice, like, and might try differently.
Good describing sentences name something specific, not just "nice" or "good".
homeworkItems: Show a grown-up one piece of art from this term and use one of our sentence starters to talk about it.

teachingScript.overview: Gather all four units' work (or photos of it) for a gallery walk -- children practise the sentence starters on real classmates' work, which lands far better than a hypothetical example.

talkingPoints: Model the difference between "I like it" and a specific describing sentence using one real piece of class artwork.
Practise each sentence starter chorally as a class before children use them independently.
Ask children to explain in their own words why the vague sentence isn't as helpful.
Do a short gallery walk: children pair up and use one sentence starter each about a partner's work.

quizQuestions.question: Reflecting on art means...
options: Using words to say what we notice, like, and might try differently
Only talking about art we don't like

quizQuestions.question: Which sentence is a better describing sentence?
options: "I notice you used dabbing to make the leaves look bumpy."

flashcards.definition: Looking at art and using words to say what we notice, like, and might try differently.
A sentence that names something specific about a piece of art.

worksheetContent.title: Worksheet -- Sharing and Talking About Our Art
worksheetContent.instructions: Choose one piece of your own art from this term to talk about.

questions.prompt: Finish this sentence: "I notice that in my art, I..."
Finish this sentence: "I like... because..."
Finish this sentence: "Next time I would..."
